subtitle: Build the Developer-7 GeoOps project from scratch, one cumulative set at a time.

books.title: GeoOps from Scratch
books.subtitle: Java 17, Spring Boot and real developer-tool workflow built cumulatively.

repositories.name: Developer-7-Intellij
repositories.description: GeoOps developer playback rebuilt set by set in IntelliJ

workflows.name: GeoOps CI
workflows.yaml:
name: GeoOps CI
on:
  push:
    branches: [ "main" ]
  pull_request:
    branches: [ "main" ]
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-java@v4
        with:
          distribution: temurin
          java-version: "17"
          cache: maven
      - run: python scripts/build-player-data.py --validate-only
      - run: mvn --batch-mode clean verify

runs.name: GeoOps CI
runs.summary: Set 1 build, test and curriculum validation passed.

stages.title: 1: Set 1 — Development Environment & Spring Boot Bootstrap
stages.subtitle: Create the first runnable GeoOps slice and carry it from project generation through CI.

steps.title: Choose Maven as the GeoOps build system
steps.why:
Alright, this is our first real project choice.

We're going with Maven.

Maven is going to help us manage the libraries GeoOps needs, run tests, and build the application.

The important file to remember is pom.xml. That's where we'll tell Maven which Java version we're using and which dependencies belong in the project.

Without Maven, we'd end up downloading JAR files and managing them ourselves. We don't want that.

So for this project, Maven becomes our build tool.

steps.title: Keep the implementation language on Java
steps.why:
Next, we choose the language we're actually going to write.

For GeoOps, that's Java.

That means the classes we create later—our controller, service, request object, and domain object—will all be Java files.

Spring Initializr could generate Kotlin or Groovy too, but that's not what this project is about.

So this option is simply telling the generator: build me a Java Spring Boot project.

steps.title: Select Java 17
steps.why:
Now let's choose the Java version.

We're using Java 17.

This choice matters because IntelliJ, Maven, and GitHub Actions should all use the same Java version.

If your laptop builds with one Java version and CI builds with another, you can get annoying “works on my machine” problems.

So we're fixing the version now and keeping GeoOps on Java 17 everywhere.

steps.title: Give the application its GeoOps identity
steps.why:
Okay, now we're giving the project its identity.

The group is com.atlasgrid and the artifact is geoops.

Together, those values help Maven identify this application.

The package name is com.atlasgrid.geoops, and you'll see that exact package at the top of our Java classes later.

So we're not just filling in a form here. These values are going to show up throughout the project structure.

data.name: GeoOps
data.description: Fictional GIS operations platform used for Java/Spring Boot experience learning

steps.title: Add Spring Web
steps.why:
Now we're adding the dependency that gives GeoOps a web API.

That dependency is Spring Web.

Once this is included, Spring Boot can run an embedded Tomcat server and our Java code can receive HTTP requests.

That's what will let us create endpoints such as GET /api/projects and POST /api/projects.

Without Spring Web, our application could still run Java code, but it would not yet be the REST application we're trying to build.

steps.title: Add Bean Validation
steps.why:
Next, we're adding Validation.

We're going to receive project data from an HTTP request, and we don't want to accept things like an empty project code or an empty project name.

This dependency gives us annotations such as @NotBlank.

Instead of writing manual checks everywhere, we can put the rule directly on the request fields.

Later, when we create CreateProjectRequest, you'll see exactly where this dependency gets used.

steps.title: Add Lombok
steps.why:
Here we're adding Lombok.

We're not using Lombok because Java is impossible without it. We're using it to remove a little repetitive code where it makes sense.

In this set, the useful example will be @Slf4j.

That annotation gives ProjectService a logger without us manually declaring the logger field.

So keep Lombok in mind; we'll connect this dependency to real code shortly.

steps.title: Generate the starter project
steps.why:
Alright, we've selected the basic project settings and dependencies, so now we generate the project.

Think of this as Spring Initializr creating the starting folder structure and pom.xml for us.

One detail: the current simulator shows a newer Spring Boot patch version, but the original Developer-7 Set 1 used Spring Boot 3.3.5.

We're rebuilding that original project order, so when we open pom.xml in IntelliJ, we'll pin it back to 3.3.5.

The goal is to reproduce the original GeoOps project, not quietly change its history.

steps.title: Open GeoOps in IntelliJ
steps.why:
Now we're moving into the tool we'll use for most of the project: IntelliJ IDEA.

From this point, this is where we'll create Java files, run tests, inspect Maven, start Spring Boot, and later debug or refactor code.

Notice that the project is still small.

That's intentional.

We're going to grow the same GeoOps project set by set instead of opening a finished codebase and pretending we built it.

steps.title: Bind IntelliJ to the Java 17 JDK
steps.why:
Before we start coding, look at the Project SDK.

We're setting it to Java 17.

The JDK is what gives IntelliJ the Java compiler and the standard Java libraries needed to build this code.

So the Java 17 choice we made in Spring Initializr is now being matched inside IntelliJ.

This is one of those setup details that saves us from version problems later.

steps.title: Create the canonical GeoOps pom.xml
steps.why:
Now we're looking at one of the most important files in a Maven project: pom.xml.

This file tells Maven what the project is and what it depends on.

At the top, we're using Spring Boot 3.3.5.

Then we add Spring Web, Validation, Actuator, Lombok, and the Spring Boot test starter.

Notice we are not manually writing a version beside every Spring dependency. Spring Boot manages compatible versions for us.

So whenever you hear “Maven dependency management,” this file is where that becomes real.

data.content:
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<project xmlns="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0"
         xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
         xsi:schemaLocation="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0 https://maven.apache.org/xsd/maven-4.0.0.xsd">
    <modelVersion>4.0.0</modelVersion>
    <parent>
        <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-parent</artifactId>
        <version>3.3.5</version>
        <relativePath/>
    </parent>
    <groupId>com.atlasgrid</groupId>
    <artifactId>geoops</artifactId>
    <version>0.0.1-SNAPSHOT</version>
    <name>GeoOps</name>
    <description>Fictional GIS operations platform used for Java/Spring Boot experience learning</description>
    <properties>
        <java.version>17</java.version>
    </properties>
    <dependencies>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
        </dependency>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-validation</artifactId>
        </dependency>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-actuator</artifactId>
        </dependency>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.projectlombok</groupId>
            <artifactId>lombok</artifactId>
            <optional>true</optional>
        </dependency>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-test</artifactId>
            <scope>test</scope>
        </dependency>
    </dependencies>
    <build>
        <plugins>
            <plugin>
                <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
                <artifactId>spring-boot-maven-plugin</artifactId>
            </plugin>
        </plugins>
    </build>
</project>

steps.title: Look up Spring Web in Maven Central
steps.why:
Let's quickly step outside IntelliJ and look at Maven Central.

When pom.xml says we need spring-boot-starter-web, Maven has to get that library from somewhere.

Maven Central is one of the remote repositories where those artifacts are published.

The first time Maven needs a dependency, it downloads it.

After that, Maven normally keeps a local copy under the .m2 repository on your machine.

So the flow is basically: pom.xml → Maven → remote repository → local .m2 cache.

steps.title: Open the Maven tool window
steps.why:
Back in IntelliJ, we're opening the Maven tool window.

This lets us see the Maven project from inside the IDE.

We can inspect dependencies and run Maven goals without leaving IntelliJ.

But here's the important point: IntelliJ is not replacing Maven.

Maven is still the build tool. IntelliJ is just giving us a convenient way to work with it.

That matters because the same Maven build should also work later in GitHub Actions.

steps.title: Walk through the Maven lifecycle
steps.why:
Now look at these Maven phases.

They happen in an order.

validate checks the project, compile compiles the Java code, test runs tests, package creates the JAR, verify performs verification, install puts the built artifact into your local Maven repository, and deploy can publish it somewhere remote.

You don't normally run every word one by one.

For example, when we run verify, Maven also goes through the earlier phases it needs first.

So think of the lifecycle as one build path with several checkpoints.

steps.title: Create the Spring Boot entry point
steps.why:
Alright, this is where our GeoOps application actually begins.

Every Java program needs an entry point, and here that entry point is main().

But notice we're not manually creating controllers, starting Tomcat, or loading every Spring class ourselves. We hand that work to Spring Boot with SpringApplication.run().

Now look at @SpringBootApplication. This tells Spring Boot that this is the main application class and that it should start configuration, auto-configuration, and component scanning.

So when this file runs, the flow is basically:

main() → SpringApplication.run() → Spring starts → embedded Tomcat starts → GeoOps is running.

At this point the application can start, but it still doesn't know what a GeoOps project looks like. That's what we'll create next.

steps.title: Model one GIS project
steps.why:
Now let's create the object that represents an actual GeoOps project.

For this first version, a project has an id, project code, name, coordinate reference system, and creation time.

The GIS-specific field here is coordinateReferenceSystem.

For example, one project might use EPSG:4326.

We're using a Java record because this object is mainly carrying data and we want it to stay simple.

Also notice what is missing: no database annotations, no PostGIS geometry, no persistence layer.

We haven't earned those parts of the architecture yet, so we're not adding them early.

steps.title: Separate request input from domain state
steps.why:
Now we need to think about what the client is allowed to send us.

A client creating a project should provide the project code, name, and coordinate reference system.

It should not choose the UUID or the creation time. Those belong to the server.

That's why we're creating CreateProjectRequest separately from GeoProject.

The @NotBlank annotations come from the Validation dependency we added earlier.

So if somebody sends an empty project code, Spring can reject the request before bad data reaches our service logic.

steps.title: Add the first GeoOps service
steps.why:
Okay, now this is an important change in the structure.

We could put project creation directly inside ProjectController, and for a tiny demo it would work.

But GeoOps is supposed to keep growing.

So we're creating ProjectService and putting the application logic there.

The controller will handle HTTP. The service will handle the work.

For now, the service stores projects in an ArrayList because we have not introduced a database yet.

And here's where Lombok finally connects to the code: @Slf4j gives this service a logger.

steps.title: Expose project intake over HTTP
steps.why:
Now we're giving GeoOps an actual HTTP entry point.

@RestController tells Spring that this class receives web requests and returns response data.

@RequestMapping("/api/projects") gives everything in this controller the same base path.

Then GET /api/projects reads projects, while POST /api/projects creates one.

Notice that the controller does not create the project itself. It passes the work to ProjectService.

So our flow is now:

HTTP request → ProjectController → ProjectService.

Later, when the project really needs a database, that flow can grow without turning this controller into one giant class.

steps.title: Configure the GeoOps runtime
steps.why:
Now we're moving a few settings out of Java code and into application.yml.

First, we give the Spring application its name: geoops.

Then we keep the local server on port 8080.

We're also exposing Actuator health and info endpoints.

That health endpoint is going to be useful in a minute because it gives us a quick way to ask, “Is the application actually running?”

So this file is basically where runtime configuration starts living.

data.content:
spring:
  application:
    name: geoops

server:
  port: 8080

management:
  endpoints:
    web:
      exposure:
        include: health,info

info:
  app:
    name: GeoOps
    domain: GIS operations
    company: AtlasGrid Geospatial Systems

steps.title: Add a Spring Boot context test
steps.why:
Before we run the whole application manually, let's add one basic test.

@SpringBootTest tells Spring to start the application context for the test.

The method itself looks almost empty, and that's okay.

What we're checking is whether Spring can load the project with the configuration and classes we've created so far.

If something important is wired incorrectly, this simple test can fail before we even open Postman.

Later sets will add more specific tests when we have more behavior to test.

steps.title: Run the JUnit test
steps.why:
Alright, let's run the test.

Watch the result at the bottom.

contextLoads is green, which means Spring was able to create the application context successfully.

That doesn't mean every possible feature is perfect.

It means our current project setup is valid enough for Spring to start.

That's exactly the checkpoint we wanted before moving on.

steps.title: Run Maven clean verify
steps.why:
Now we're going one step beyond the IntelliJ test button.

We're running Maven clean verify.

clean removes the old build output, and verify builds the project and runs the tests through Maven's lifecycle.

Why do this if the test already passed in IntelliJ?

Because we want proof that the project builds through Maven itself, not only through the IDE.

The BUILD SUCCESS message is what we want to see before the same command eventually runs in CI.

data.console:
[INFO] Compiling GeoOps with Java 17
[INFO] Running GeoOpsApplicationTests
[INFO] Tests run: 1, Failures: 0, Errors: 0
[INFO] BUILD SUCCESS

steps.title: Start GeoOps from IntelliJ
steps.why:
Okay, now let's actually start GeoOps.

This time we're not just testing the Spring context. We're running the application.

main() starts, SpringApplication.run() takes over, Spring creates the application context, and embedded Tomcat starts on port 8080.

Once you see the “Started GeoOpsApplication” message, the server is ready to receive HTTP requests.

So now we can leave IntelliJ for a moment and talk to the application from Postman.

data.name: GeoOpsApplication
data.console: 2026-09-29 INFO Starting GeoOpsApplication using Java 17\n2026-09-29 INFO Tomcat started on port 8080 (http)\n2026-09-29 INFO Started GeoOpsApplication

steps.title: Open the Actuator health request
steps.why:
Before we test project creation, let's check something simpler.

We're opening GET /actuator/health.

We didn't write this endpoint in ProjectController. Actuator gives it to us because of the dependency we added earlier.

Think of this as asking the application one basic question:

“Are you up?”

If this health request fails, there is no point debugging our project API yet. We would first make sure Spring Boot is actually running.

steps.title: Confirm GeoOps is healthy
steps.why:
There it is: 200 OK and status UP.

That tells us GeoOps is running and reachable on port 8080.

This is our first request coming from outside IntelliJ into the Spring Boot application.

So the path is now:

Postman → Tomcat → Spring Boot → Actuator.

Next we'll do the same thing with an endpoint that we actually wrote ourselves.

steps.title: Open the Create Project request
steps.why:
Now we're opening the request that creates a GeoOps project.

The method is POST and the URL is /api/projects.

Look at the JSON body.

We're sending projectCode, name, and coordinateReferenceSystem because those are the fields in CreateProjectRequest.

For the CRS we're using EPSG:4326, which keeps the example tied to the GIS domain.

When we send this, the request should go through the controller and into ProjectService.

steps.title: Create the first GIS intake record
steps.why:
Now watch the full flow happen.

Postman sends the JSON to ProjectController.

Spring validates CreateProjectRequest, then the controller passes it to ProjectService.

The service generates the UUID and creation time, stores the GeoProject in memory, and returns it.

The response is 201 Created, which is exactly what we expect when a new resource is created.

So this one request proves several pieces are connected:

Postman → Controller → Validation → Service → GeoProject → JSON response.

steps.title: Open the project list request
steps.why:
We created a project, so now let's check whether GeoOps can return it.

This request is GET /api/projects.

There is no request body this time because we're simply asking for the projects the service currently knows about.

Inside the application, ProjectController calls ProjectService.findAll().

Remember, we're still using the in-memory list from Set 1.

So this request is reading from that same temporary list.

steps.title: Read the project back from GeoOps
steps.why:
And there is the Austin project we created earlier.

That means our first create-and-read flow is working.

One important limitation: this project only lives in memory right now.

If we stop the application and start it again, this record disappears.

That's not a bug in this set. We simply have not introduced a database yet.

When persistence becomes part of the learning order, we'll replace this temporary storage properly instead of pretending a database exists today.

steps.title: Open the working tree in Git
steps.why:
The code works locally, so now let's look at the Git side.

Git is going to track how this project changes over time.

Right now these files are new or modified in our working tree.

Think of the working tree as the current state of the files on our machine.

Nothing has been recorded as a permanent Git commit yet.

Before we commit, we'll decide which changes belong in that snapshot.

steps.title: Stage the Set 1 files
steps.why:
Now we're staging the Set 1 files.

Staging means, “These are the changes I want in my next commit.”

This gives us a chance to review what we're about to record.

For this first milestone, the Java source, configuration, test, Maven file, and CI workflow all belong together.

So we stage them as one complete GeoOps starting point.

steps.title: Commit the GeoOps bootstrap
steps.why:
Now we create the commit.

The message is “Complete Set 1 GeoOps bootstrap.”

A commit is basically a saved point in the project's history.

Later, when Set 2 adds new code, we'll be able to see exactly what changed from this Set 1 version.

That's why we're not treating Git as something we use only at the end of a project.

We're recording the project as it grows.

steps.title: Push Set 1 to the remote
steps.why:
The commit exists locally, but GitHub doesn't know about it yet.

So now we push main to the remote repository.

This sends our Git history from the local machine to GitHub.

After the push, other tools can react to that repository change.

In our case, GitHub Actions can run the build automatically, and the learning site deployment can also use the repository.

So this is the point where local development becomes shared repository state.

data.output: Enumerating objects... done.\nTo https://github.com/sabareeshrao/Developer-7-Intellij.git\n   set1001  main -> main

steps.title: Open Developer-7-Intellij on GitHub
steps.why:
Now we're looking at Developer-7-Intellij on GitHub.

This is the remote copy of the project we just pushed.

The Java project lives here, but this repository also contains the curriculum that drives the simulator.

The actual simulator software still comes from Experiment-VS-Code.

So the relationship is simple:

Experiment-VS-Code provides the reusable software simulation.

Developer-7-Intellij provides the GeoOps project and the learning steps.

steps.title: Open GitHub Actions
steps.why:
Next, let's look at GitHub Actions.

This is our CI area.

Whenever we push code, the workflow can start on a fresh GitHub runner.

It sets up Java 17, validates the learning curriculum, and runs Maven clean verify.

That is important because it answers a simple question:

“Can this project build successfully somewhere other than my own IntelliJ setup?”

steps.title: Inspect the successful Set 1 CI run
steps.why:
And this is the final checkpoint for Set 1.

The GitHub Actions run is green.

So we have now gone through the whole developer flow:

Spring Initializr → IntelliJ → Java code → JUnit → Maven → Spring Boot → Postman → Git → GitHub → GitHub Actions.

More importantly, we did it with one project that now has a real starting history.

Set 2 will continue from this exact GeoOps codebase. We're not starting over.
